title: Adolescence: Charms and Challenges
summary: Adolescence is the period between childhood and adulthood, from about 10 to 19 years, marked by physical, emotional, social and cognitive changes started by hormones; they prepare adolescents for adult roles and should be accepted. Physical development begins with puberty (sexual maturity); about 75% of adult height and 50% of adult weight are gained. Common changes: increase in height and weight, underarm and pubic hair, pimples, development of reproductive organs. Boys: broadening of shoulders, deepening of voice, facial hair, muscular development, nocturnal emission. Girls: growth of breasts, broadening of hips, menarche.

Menstruation (menarche between 9 and 16 years; menopause around 45–55) is a cycle of about 28 days; one ovum matures and is released at ovulation mid-cycle; the uterus builds up a lining and, if the ovum is not fertilised, sheds it as the menstrual flow of blood, mucus and tissue. A girl who has not begun menstruating by 16 should see a doctor. A girl can get pregnant before her first period. Irregularity is common at first; stress, illness and poor nutrition upset the cycle; iron-rich food prevents anaemia. Myths and facts: girls should continue daily activities (walking and exercise ease cramps); menstruation is natural; avoid medicines to delay or hasten it; bathe daily (a warm bath soothes cramps); women can enter the kitchen, handle pickle and take part in religious functions; use clean sanitary napkins changed every six hours, or clean cloth washed with soap and dried in the sun. Nocturnal emission (wet dreams) is natural; it does not cause weakness, is not always linked to sexual thoughts, and not all boys experience it. Genital hygiene for both sexes: wash with clean water after urination, wear cotton undergarments, change at least daily and sun-dry them, change stained ones at once, keep pubic hair trimmed.

Emotional development is the ability to manage and express emotions in positive and responsible ways; mood swings and rebellion are common. Respond to anger by recognising the signals, diverting yourself, doing something constructive, analysing the cause and seeking help from trusted people; sensible response is to talk and clear misunderstanding. Self concept is the way you see your strengths and weaknesses (high when you look at strengths); self-esteem is your judgment of your abilities. To build positive self-esteem: accept strong points and weaknesses, accept what cannot be changed, avoid self-pity, seek advice, eat healthy and exercise.

Social development: adolescents seek identity and independence, value peers (approval, even changing behaviour to win it), and want privacy. Good parent–adolescent relations: open communication, listen and respect, courtesy to own parents. Peer pressure can be positive (social development, self-esteem, role models, healthy behaviour such as sports) or negative (isolated teens may take to thefts, substance abuse, smoking, drinking). Healthy peer relations need effective communication, anger management, fairness, empathy, spending time, constructive criticism, generosity and no bullying.

Cognitive development: abstract thinking (can imagine the impossible, understand idioms and humour); personal fable (think they are unique and nothing bad can happen, so they take risks); systematic thinking (list and examine alternatives and their consequences); idealism (strong sense of right and wrong); imaginary audience (think everyone is watching them, e.g. a small hole in the T-shirt).

Social norms are the rules and expectations by which a society guides its members' behaviour; gender roles change. Adolescents copy popular language, clothes, music and dance. To say no assertively: do not give in because everyone is doing it; say 'no' rather than 'I can't'; do not feel guilty or say sorry; keep body language and eye contact firm; do not give reasons for every action; maintain dignity; techniques – ignore and walk off, change the topic, assertively say no. Media (TV, newspapers, magazines, films, radio, internet) create awareness and opportunities but promote stereotypes, sexual images and violence; actors and models shape ideas of the perfect body, leading to eating disorders, obsessive weight training and steroid use (loss of stamina, lower resistance, irregular periods); parents help by separating fantasy and reality, discussing consequences of violence and risk taking and teaching critical thinking and age-appropriate viewing. Career: start preparing early, explore options, use newspapers, guidance websites, parents and professionals, and internships or on-the-job training.

objective: State True or False: (i) Parents can help reduce the negative effects of media on their children. (ii) Social norms are a set of rules and expectations by which society guides the behaviour of its members. (iii) Adolescents look to their parents for approval and even change their behaviour to win their approval. (iv) Girls should remain indoors during menstruation.
(i) True. (ii) True. (iii) False – they look to their peers for approval. (iv) False – they should continue daily activities.

vsa: Teenagers' ideal body shape is influenced by actors and models. What are the four negative effects of this on their health?

Eating disorders from excessive dieting; loss of stamina and decreased resistance to disease; irregular menstrual cycles in girls; obsessive weight training and use of steroids and supplements in boys with harmful effects.
Your friend has stopped eating regular meals as she wants to look slim like film stars. Give four suggestions to help her.

Tell her that actors and models are not a realistic ideal; explain that crash dieting causes weakness, loss of stamina, poor resistance and irregular periods; encourage a balanced diet and exercise; build her self-esteem by accepting her body; limit exposure to such media and seek a doctor's or counsellor's advice.
How are teenagers impacted by media and fashion? Give four examples.

They copy popular language, clothes, music and dance; they idolise stars and may lose their individuality; their idea of a perfect body shape changes, leading to dieting and eating disorders; exposure to violence and sexual images affects them negatively; media can also motivate them to take up sports and social work.
Give two suggestions each to help Neha improve her relationship with her mother (two for Neha, two for the mother).

Neha: talk openly and respect her mother's point of view; help in household chores and talk courteously. Mother: involve Neha in family discussions and trust her; talk openly, understand and counsel her.
What is meant by self concept and self-esteem?
Self concept is the way you see your strengths and weaknesses; self-esteem is your personal judgment of your abilities. A positive self concept leads to higher self-esteem.
Explain 'peer' and give two positive effects of positive peer pressure.

A peer is a person of equal age, abilities, qualifications, background or social status. Positive peer pressure helps social development and self-esteem, gives a safety net in difficult times, provides role models and encourages healthy behaviour such as sports.
Write any four tips for maintaining genital hygiene in adolescence.

Wash with clean water after urination; use cotton undergarments; change undergarments daily and dry them in the sun; change stained garments at once; keep pubic hair trimmed; use clean sanitary napkins changed every six hours.
Mention four ways to say 'no' assertively to peer pressure.

Use the word 'no' rather than 'I can't'; do not feel guilty or say sorry; keep eye contact and consistent body language; change the topic, ignore the question and walk off, or assertively convince; do not give reasons for every action.
sa: Make the girls aware of any three myths and facts regarding menstruation.

Myth: girls should not work during menstruation – Fact: they should continue daily activities; walking and exercise relieve cramps. Myth: bathing causes cramps – Fact: a warm bath soothes muscles; bathe daily. Myth: women should not enter the kitchen or handle pickle – Fact: there is no scientific evidence for such restrictions. Myth: it is alright to take medicine to delay periods – Fact: avoid it without a doctor's advice.
Describe the cognitive characteristics of adolescents with an example of each (any three).

Abstract thinking – they can imagine the impossible and understand idioms and humour. Personal fable – they think they are unique and nothing bad can happen, so they take risks. Systematic thinking – they can list alternatives and their consequences, e.g. planning a holiday. Idealism – a strong sense of right and wrong. Imaginary audience – they think everyone is watching them, e.g. a small hole in the T-shirt.
Explain how parents can reduce the negative effect of media on adolescents.

Help them distinguish fantasy from reality; discuss the consequences of violence and risk-taking behaviour; empower them with critical thinking and decision-making skills so they filter messages and watch age-appropriate content.
la: Give five suggestions to adolescents to deal with negative peer pressure.

(1) Do not give in because everyone else is doing it. (2) Say 'no' firmly rather than 'I can't', without guilt. (3) Keep body language and eye contact consistent with the words. (4) Use techniques such as changing the topic or walking away. (5) Do not give reasons for every action and maintain your dignity. (6) Choose friends who encourage healthy behaviour and share problems with parents or trusted persons. (7) Practise assertive skills before the situation arises.
Write any five physical changes in adolescent girls.
Increase in height and weight; growth of breasts; broadening of hips; growth of underarm and pubic hair; pimples or acne; development of reproductive organs; menarche (start of menstruation).

or: Suggest any five ways to develop self-esteem in adolescents.

Accept strong points and appreciate them; acknowledge weaknesses and work on them; accept physical aspects that cannot be changed; avoid self-pity; seek advice from a trusted friend, parent or counsellor; appreciate others honestly; eat healthy and exercise; take pride in abilities and success.
